Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Destructive disinfection of infected brood prevents systemic disease spread in ant colonies" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Rebeca Rosengaus (Reviewer #1).

Our decision has been reached after consultation between the reviewers. Based on these discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife.

The main point that led to the reject decision is not so evident from the text of the reviews, but became clear in the discussion session. Although the paper presents interesting and very careful work, it does not provide a big step forward in the field, in particular not in light of your previous publications on this topic. Although the destructive disinfection was considered to be novel, its exact mechanism is not very clear. As pointed out in review #1, the CHC profile would need to be further studied to ensure where it comes from. In fact, since this is the crucial signal, it would require deeper analysis to understand how it comes about. If it emanates indeed from the pupae, it would constitute an early phase immune response that would need to be clarified in more depth. In case you can substantially improve the paper on this aspect, you are welcome to submit a new version.

Reviewer #1:

This is an interesting manuscript in which the authors studied a previously unreported behaviour of "destructive disinfection" of ant pupae by Lasius workers. The authors report on serially linked behavioural acts that involve the removal of fungally infected pupae from its cocoon, followed by the perforation of the pupa's cuticle and finally the administration of poison secretions with antimicrobial properties. These coupled tasks ultimately reduce the risk of disease transmission/infection within a colony. The authors did a nice job in systematically addressing and tackling many of the aspects involved in this novel behaviour. Their methods, sample sizes and data analyses provide convincing evidence that this behaviour is inducible and adaptive. My major concern lays on the experimental design of the CHC. It appears the authors did not run chemical signature analyses on the triton+conidia suspension only? If this is the case, then they cannot ascertain that the changes in CHC profile of infected pupae represents "sickness cues" given off by the pupae. The possibility exists that those changes are of fungal (and not ant) origin. Given this and several other minor concerns, I cannot recommend this work for publication in its present form. Below some suggestions and hopefully constructive criticisms that I think may improve the clarity of their work. A pleasure reading such thorough research.

Reviewer #2:

Overview

Social insects have served for the past two decades as models to understand the evolution of immunocompetence (in the broad sense) in animal societies. Many social insect species face significant immune challenges due to their densely populated and large colonies in which disease transmission can be facilitated. Hymenopteran species may be genetically compromised due to haplodiploidy, and polyandrous mating may enhance worker disease resistance. Social immunity involves colony-level prophylactic response (sanitation) and/or the upregulation of immune factors related to vaccination-like effects resulting from social interactions, collectively reducing infection risk.

Current submission

In the present study, Lasius neglectus ants are described as using "destructive disinfection" to limit disease transmission of a fungal pathogen by removing pupae within which the pathogen is undergoing non-contagious incubation. Workers appear to be able to detect chemical cues emitted by pupae, recognizing disease risk and treating such pupae with antimicrobial secretions from the poison gland.

Evaluation

Colonies of social insects are known to identify, and sanitize, by allogrooming and/or antimicrobial secretion distribution, and/or remove infected larvae or workers, elevating colony temperature and generating "fever" and/or signalling the presence of pathogens following their detection. The authors' work extends our understanding of how individuals may serve immune-cell like functions to achieve colony-level resistance to disease. The finding that "the same principles of disease defence apply at different levels of biological organization" does not in and of itself appear to be unusual and/or highly novel and unexpected; it is a well-used superorganism analogy. As the authors note, previous studies have shown that workers (of several social insect species) remove infected brood. I do not see the response now reported to be substantially different in terms of how it advances our understanding of infection control in animal societies, although the authors coin a new term for their phenomenon. Overall, the "multicomponent behaviour' appears to be to remove infected individuals and sanitize them, killing them in the process (intentionally or unintentionally). This category of response to infection has been previously been shown in other social insects, for example, in the general context of undertaking behaviour. A more novel and significant result would be if workers did not destructively disinfect, but rather identified pre-contagious pupae and "medically" treated them with poison gland secretion, improving their survival.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Destructive disinfection of infected brood prevents systemic disease spread in ant colonies" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favourably evaluated by Diethard Tautz (Reviewing editor) and two reviewers.

The reviewers have no further comments on the experimental side, but reviewer #2 (and after the discussion of these comments reviewer #1 agreed to them as well) suggests putting the results into a broader context. Please look through your text (i.e. Introduction/Discussion) and include these perspectives where it seems appropriate.

Reviewer #1:

The authors have addressed all my concerns and I believe that adding those extra experiments on the CHC has made this a robust and complete contribution to the field of social insect eco-immunology. I recommend this work for publication in its current form.

Reviewer #2:

In their revised manuscript, the authors have effectively responded to reviewer comments by adding new data and refining the narrative. The new studies add details absent in the initial submission that demonstrate chemicals used to disinfect brood are not of fungal origin, and workers thus detect cues associated with disease symptoms. Independent of the potential impact of the study in the broader analysis of social immunocompetence, the work is rigorous, advances our understanding of mechanisms underpinning social responses to infection control, and is to be applauded. However, the question remains as to whether adding details of the mechanisms regulating the disinfection process in ants is broadly significant or serves a more specialized audience. Here it can also be noted that the first sentence of the revised Abstract focuses the study in social insect biology, rather than the broader ecological immunology of animal social systems, and "completing the (superorganism) analogy" similarly accentuates insect sociobiology. My sense is that most practitioners in the field would agree that "the same principles of disease defence apply at different levels of biological organization" is already understood, at the level of analogy. The authors draw parallels and note variation among honey bee and ant systems of disease control. The more general message for the analysis of social and ecological immunology should be clarified. For example, aside from the mechanistic details, do the present results offer deeper insights into the concept of herd immunity, applied across diverse taxa? If so, the authors should state so clearly, as it this would be more informative than "completing the superorganism analogy."

claims.source: These defences are performed collectively by the workers to form an emergent layer of protection known as social immunity that, like the immune system of a body, protects the colony from invading pathogens (Cremer et al., 2007; Rosengaus et al., 2011; Cremer et al., 2017; Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an established concept in social insect biology, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sanitary care in ants involves grooming and the use of antimicrobial secretions to mechanically remove and chemically disinfect pathogens.
claims.source: In ants, sanitary care involves grooming and the use of antimicrobial secretions to mechanically remove and chemically disinfect pathogens, reducing the likelihood that pathogen exposure leads to the development of an infection (Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ant sanitary care, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Social immunity is characterised by a care-kill dichotomy, where colony members should be cared for when possible but sacrificed if necessary.
claims.source: Hence, social immunity is characterised by a care-kill dichotomy, where colony members should be cared for when possible but sacrificed if necessary, both of which benefit the colony (Cremer et al., 2017; Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical framework for understanding social immunity, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The kill-component is a unique feature of social immunity that is not present in the disease defence repertoire of other forms of sociality.
claims.source: Although the kill-component is an unique feature of social immunity that is not present in the disease defence repertoire of other forms of sociality (e.g. non-superorganismal family groups, communal breeders or aggregations [Cremer et al., 2017]), it is rarely studied in comparison to the care-component.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the uniqueness of social immunity, supported by citation.

claims.claim: What happens when sanitary care fails and a pathogen successfully infects a colony member remains poorly understood.
claims.source: Hence, what happens when sanitary care fails and a pathogen successfully infects a colony member, with the consequent potential to create an epidemic, remains poorly understood (but see [Rothenbuhler, 1964; Ugelvig et al., 2010; Tragust et al., 2013b]).
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge, with citations to limited prior work.

claims.claim: Infections should be detected quickly and accurately by nestmates to overcome the pathogen before it has time to replicate and produce propagules that can infect others.
claims.source: To effectively protect the colony, we predict that infections should be detected quickly and accurately by nestmates, in order to overcome the pathogen before it has time to replicate and produce propagules that can infect others.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning about effective disease control.

claims.claim: The colony should respond by eliminating the infection as effectively as possible, by preventing any further opportunities for disease transmission.
claims.source: Once detected, the colony should respond by eliminating the infection as effectively as possible, by preventing any further opportunities for disease transmission.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning about effective disease control.

claims.claim: Fungus-infected ants become highly contagious to nestmates after death and can cause epidemics that result in colony collapse.
claims.source: For example, previous studies have shown that fungus-infected ants become highly contagious to nestmates after death and can cause epidemics that result in colony collapse (Hughes et al., 2002; Loreto and Hughes, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: When Metarhizium infectious conidiospores come into contact with insect cuticle, they attach, germinate and penetrate the host cuticle within 24–48 hr to cause internal infections.
claims.source: When the infectious conidiospores of this fungus come into contact with insect cuticle, they attach, germinate and penetrate the host cuticle within 24–48 hr to cause internal infections (Vestergaard et al., 1999; Walker and Hughes, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium infection biology, supported by citations.

claims.claim: During a short, non-infectious incubation period following Metarhizium infection, the fungus goes through a single-cell blastospore stage, which lasts 1–2 days.
claims.source: During a short, non-infectious incubation period following infection, the fungus goes through a single-cell blastospore stage, which lasts 1–2 days.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium lifecycle.

claims.claim: Once the host has died from Metarhizium infection, the fungus enters a saprophytic mycelial phase, then grows out of the corpse 1–3 days later, releasing millions of new infectious conidiospores in a process called sporulation.
claims.source: Once the host has died, the fungus enters a saprophytic mycelial phase, then grows out of the corpse, 1–3 days later, releasing millions of new infectious conidiospores, in a process called sporulation (Hughes et al., 2002; Deacon, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium lifecycle, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Brood infected with Metarhizium is removed from the brood chamber.
claims.source: Previous work found that brood infected with Metarhizium is removed from the brood chamber (Ugelvig et al., 2010; Tragust et al., 2013b), however, it is unknown how the ants then respond to the infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Ants tending pathogen-exposed pupae prematurely removed the pupae from their cocoons in a behaviour termed 'unpacking', whereas control pupae were left cocooned.
claims.source: We observed that ants tending pathogen-exposed pupae prematurely removed the pupae from their cocoons in a behaviour we termed 'unpacking', whereas control pupae were left cocooned (Figure 1A–B, Video 1; Cox proportional hazards regression: likelihood ratio test (LR) χ2= 55.48, df = 3, p<0.001; hazard ratios (x greater chance of unpacking compared to control): low dose = 18, medium = 53, high = 111; post-hoc comparisons: control vs. low, p=0.004; low vs. medium, p=0.006; medium vs. high = 0.024; all others, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1A-B and Video 1.

claims.claim: Unpacking occurred between 2 and 10 days after pathogen exposure, but sooner and more frequently at higher conidiospore dosages.
claims.source: Unpacking occurred between 2 and 10 days after pathogen exposure, but sooner and more frequently at higher conidiospore dosages (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The ants were unable to remove any conidiospores from the majority of the cocoons or the unpacked pupae at the time of unpacking.
claims.source: As unpacking was a belated response to pathogen exposure and we were unable to remove any conidiospores from the majority of the cocoons or the unpacked pupae (number of colony forming units [mean ± 95% CIs]: cocoons = 0.6 ± 0.9; pupae = 0.1 ± 0.35; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we concluded that the ants were not performing unpacking to simply dispose of contaminated cocoons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data on CFU counts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: On average across the conidiospore dosages, 85% of unpacked pupae harboured infections that sporulated in the absence of the ants.
claims.source: We found that, on average across the conidiospore dosages, 85% of unpacked pupae harboured infections that sporulated in the absence of the ants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from incubation experiments.

claims.claim: Only 25% of non-unpacked pupae were infected.
claims.source: In contrast, only 25% of non-unpacked pupae were infected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; generalised linear model [GLM]: overall LR χ2 = 26.48, df = 5, p<0.001; cocooned vs. unpacked pupae: LR χ2 = 18.5, df = 1, p=0.001; conidiospore dose: LR χ2 = 0.42, df = 2, p=0.81).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The ants were detecting and unpacking pupae with lethal infections during the asymptomatic incubation period of the pathogen's lifecycle.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that the ants were detecting and unpacking pupae with lethal infections during the asymptomatic incubation period of the pathogen's lifecycle.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that unpacked pupae had high infection rates and unpacking occurred before external symptoms.

claims.claim: At the time of unpacking, the fungus growing inside the pupae is non-infectious and essentially no viable conidiospores are leftover from the pathogen exposure on their cuticle.
claims.source: At this time point, the fungus growing inside the pupae is non-infectious and essentially no viable conidiospores are leftover from the pathogen exposure on their cuticle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), so there is very little risk of the ants contracting the disease whilst unpacking the pupae.
claims.evidence: This is supported by CFU data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and knowledge of fungal lifecycle.

claims.claim: After unpacking, the ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approximately 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care.
claims.source: The ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approx. 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care (~13 times/d; Figure 1D; generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: LR χ2 = 17.04, df = 1, p<0.001), and grooming duration doubled (Figure 1C; linear mixed effects regression [LMER]: LR χ2 = 145.26, df = 1, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Grooming duration doubled after unpacking compared to sanitary care.
claims.source: The ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approx. 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care (~13 times/d; Figure 1D; generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: LR χ2 = 17.04, df = 1, p<0.001), and grooming duration doubled (Figure 1C; linear mixed effects regression [LMER]: LR χ2 = 145.26, df = 1, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The ants repeatedly bit the pupae to make perforations in their cuticles and to remove their limbs after unpacking.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ants repeatedly bit the pupae to make perforations in their cuticles and to remove their limbs (Figure 1E; GLMM: LR χ2 = 39.44, df = 1, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The combination of unpacking, grooming, poison spraying and biting resulted in the death of the pupae and left their corpses heavily damaged and coated in the ants' poison.
claims.source: Together these three behaviours resulted in the death of the pupae and left their corpses heavily damaged and coated in the ants' poison (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by observational data and measurements shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Pentane-washed pupae showed a 72% reduction in unpacking compared to both non- and water-washed infected pupae.
claims.source: We washed infected pupae in pentane to reduce the abundance of their cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs). When pentane-washed pupae were presented to ants, there was a 72% reduction in unpacking compared to both non- and water-washed infected pupae (Figure 2A; GLM: LR χ2 = 12.2, df = 2, p=0.002; Tukey post hoc comparisons: water-washed vs. non-washed, p=0.79; all others, p=0.009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs.
claims.source: As pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), this result indicates that the ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
claims.source: As pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), this result indicates that the ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the pentane washing experiment showing reduced unpacking when CHCs are removed.

claims.claim: Unpacked pathogen-exposed pupae have distinct chemical profiles compared to sham-treated control pupae.
claims.source: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis of the solvent wash confirmed that unpacked pupae have distinct chemical profiles compared to non-infected control pupae, whilst cocooned (non-unpacked) pathogen-exposed pupae were intermediate (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; perMANOVA: F = 1.49, df = 46, p=0.002; post-hoc perMANOVA comparisons: unpacked vs. control, p=0.003; unpacked vs. cocooned, p=0.79; cocooned vs. control, p=0.08).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS chemical analysis data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2B.

claims.claim: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae.
claims.source: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these differences were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The chemical differences on infected pupae were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
claims.source: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these differences were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the absence of novel compounds and confirmed by direct comparison of fungal and pupal chemical profiles.

claims.claim: There were no fungus-derived peaks in the pupal chemical profiles.
claims.source: By analysing the chemical profiles of each of the pathogen's separate developmental stages (infectious conidiospores, post-infection blastospores, and saprophytic mycelium) and performing a direct comparison of the fungal compounds to the pupal chemical profiles, we confirmed that there were no fungus-derived peaks in the pupal profiles (see Materials and methods for more information).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative chemical analysis of fungal and pupal profiles.

claims.claim: Eight out of the 24 CHCs identified had higher relative abundances on unpacked pupae compared to control pupae.
claims.source: Correspondingly, we found that 8 out of the 24 CHCs identified (Table 1) had higher relative abundances on unpacked pupae compared to control pupae (Figure 2C–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; all Kruskal-Wallis [KW] test statistics and post-hoc comparisons in Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures and tables.

claims.claim: Four CHCs were present in relatively higher quantities on unpacked pupae compared to the non-unpacked cocooned pupae.
claims.source: Moreover, four of these CHCs were also present in relatively higher quantities on unpacked pupae compared to the non-unpacked cocooned pupae.
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2C-F.

claims.claim: Several specific CHCs are probably accumulating on infected pupae over time, eventually reaching an amount that is sufficient to elicit destructive disinfection.
claims.source: Several specific CHCs are therefore probably accumulating on infected pupae over time, eventually reaching an amount that, relative to the other compounds, is sufficient to elicit destructive disinfection. This corresponds to current models of social insect behaviour, where the likelihood of a response depends on stimuli exceeding a certain threshold (Theraulaz et al., 1998; Beshers and Fewell, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data showing dose-dependent unpacking and CHC accumulation, combined with theoretical models cited.

claims.claim: PGRP-SC2 showed increased gene expression 48 hr after β-glucan injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection.
claims.source: However, both (B) PGRP-SC2, an IMD pathway regulator gene (Bischoff et al., 2006), and (C) β−1,3-GBP, a pattern recognition protein that specifically binds to fungal β-glucans (Ma and Kanost, 2000; Gottar et al., 2006), showed increased gene expression 48 hr after injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 17, p=0.0095; β−1,3-GBP: U = 19, p=0.01), but not following saline injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 70, p=0.06; β−1,3-GBP, saline: U = 81, p=0.0095, a significant down regulation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: β−1,3-GBP showed increased gene expression 48 hr after β-glucan injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection.
claims.source: However, both (B) PGRP-SC2, an IMD pathway regulator gene (Bischoff et al., 2006), and (C) β−1,3-GBP, a pattern recognition protein that specifically binds to fungal β-glucans (Ma and Kanost, 2000; Gottar et al., 2006), showed increased gene expression 48 hr after injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 17, p=0.0095; β−1,3-GBP: U = 19, p=0.01), but not following saline injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 70, p=0.06; β−1,3-GBP, saline: U = 81, p=0.0095, a significant down regulation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans had increased relative abundances of Tritriacontadiene (C33:2) 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection.
claims.source: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans (green dots) had increased relative abundances 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection, of (A) Tritriacontadiene, C33:2 (LMER: LR χ2 = x, df = 1, p=0.012) and (B) Tritriacontene, C33:1 (LR χ2 = 6.40, df = 1, p=0.046), but not (C) Pentatriacontadiene, C35:2 (LR χ2 = 1.56, df = 1, p=0.42) or (D) co-eluting Pentatriacontadiene and Pentatriacontene, C35:2 + C35:1 (LR χ2 = 0.25, df = 1, p=0.70).
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans had increased relative abundances of Tritriacontene (C33:1) 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection.
claims.source: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans (green dots) had increased relative abundances 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection, of (A) Tritriacontadiene, C33:2 (LMER: LR χ2 = x, df = 1, p=0.012) and (B) Tritriacontene, C33:1 (LR χ2 = 6.40, df = 1, p=0.046), but not (C) Pentatriacontadiene, C35:2 (LR χ2 = 1.56, df = 1, p=0.42) or (D) co-eluting Pentatriacontadiene and Pentatriacontene, C35:2 + C35:1 (LR χ2 = 0.25, df = 1, p=0.70).
claims.evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: Injection of β−1,3-glucans results in higher CHC abundance for two out of the four CHCs that were also specifically increased on Metarhizium-infected, unpacked pupae.
claims.source: Hence, injection of β−1,3-glucans results in higher CHC abundance for two out of the four CHCs that were also specifically increased on Metarhizium-infected, unpacked pupae (Figure 2C–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparing the β-glucan injection results with the Metarhizium infection results.

claims.claim: Some of the changes in pupal chemical profile can be directly linked to a host reaction to an immune elicitor.
claims.source: These data reveal that some of the changes in pupal chemical profile can be directly linked to a host reaction to an immune elicitor, similar to findings in honeybees (Richard et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2008), mice (Arakawa et al., 2011) and humans (Shirasu and Touhara, 2011).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the β-glucan injection experiment results, with citations to similar findings in other species.

claims.claim: Destructive disinfection significantly reduced the proportion of pupae that sporulated after 1 day by 65%.
claims.source: Whilst 88% of pupae contracted infections, destructive disinfection significantly reduced the proportion of pupae that sporulated and hence became infectious (Figure 3A; GLM: LR χ2 = 40.47, df = 2, p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparisons: 1 vs. 5 d, p=0.04; all others, p<0.001). After only 1 day, the number of destructively disinfected pupae that sporulated decreased by 65%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: With more time (5 days), the ants could reduce the number of pupae sporulating by 95%.
claims.source: With more time, the ants could reduce the number of pupae sporulating even further by 95%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Destructive disinfection permanently prevents pathogen replication.
claims.source: Since the pupae were removed from the ants for fungal incubation, we can conclude that destructive disinfection permanently prevents pathogen replication.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental design where pupae were removed from ants before incubation.

claims.claim: Smaller groups of ants (3 ants) were less efficient at destructive disinfection than larger ones (8 ants).
claims.source: We repeated this experiment with a smaller number of ants (three ants per pupae per group) to investigate how group size influences the success of destructive disinfection. Smaller groups of ants were less efficient than larger ones: although they could still inhibit >90% of pupal infections within 5 days of unpacking, pupae tested for infection after 1 day still sporulated 70% of the time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; GLM: LR χ2 = 35.23, p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparisons: 0 vs. 1 day, p=0.2; 0 vs. 5 days, p<0.001; 1 vs. 5 days, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: All three behaviours (unpacking, biting and poison spraying) must be performed in the correct order and interact to prevent pathogen replication.
claims.source: We found that all three behaviours must be performed in the correct order and interact to prevent pathogen replication (overview graph showing odds ratios of sporulation in Figure 3B, full data dataset displayed in Figure 3—figure supplement 3; GLM: overall LR χ2 = 79.9, df = 5, p<0.001; interaction between behaviours LR χ2 = 20.6, df = 2, p<0.001; all post-hoc comparisons in Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The poison is the active antimicrobial compound that inhibits fungal growth.
claims.source: As in sanitary care, the poison was the active antimicrobial compound that inhibited fungal growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Table 3, Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The cocoon is hydrophobic and prevents the aqueous poison from reaching the pupae inside.
claims.source: However, for the poison to function the pupae had to be removed from their cocoons and their cuticles damaged. Firstly, this is because the cocoon itself is hydrophobic and thus prevents the aqueous poison from reaching the pupae inside (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing pH differences in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The cuticle must be broken for the poison to enter the hemocoel of the pupae because the infection is growing internally at the time of unpacking.
claims.source: Secondly, as the infection is growing internally at the time of unpacking, the cuticle must be broken in order for the poison to enter the hemocoel of the pupae. This is achieved with the perforations created by the ants biting the pupal cuticle.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that biting is necessary for poison effectiveness.

claims.claim: The poison is probably the limiting factor determining whether destructive disinfection is successful.
claims.source: As the active antimicrobial component, we concluded that the poison is probably the limiting factor determining whether destructive disinfection is successful.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing time and group size effects.

claims.claim: The poison has a slow biosynthesis and each ant can only store a limited amount.
claims.source: Because the poison has a slow biosynthesis and each ant can only store a limited amount (Tragust et al., 2013a; Hefetz and Blum, 1978), it would explain why destructive disinfection was more likely to be successful the longer the ants had to treat the pupae, and as the number of ants increased (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from citations combined with inference from the experimental results.

claims.claim: By sharing the task of poison synthesis and application, the ants probably increase their chances of preventing the pathogen becoming infectious.
claims.source: By sharing the task of poison synthesis and application, the ants probably increase their chances of preventing the pathogen becoming infectious.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the group size effects observed in the experiments.

claims.claim: Sporulating pupae were highly virulent and caused lethal infections that became contagious after host death in 42% of ants.
claims.source: As in previous studies, sporulating corpses were highly virulent (Hughes et al., 2002; Loreto and Hughes, 2016) and caused lethal infections that became contagious after host death in 42% of ants (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There was no disease transmission from destructively disinfected pupae.
claims.source: However, there was no disease transmission from destructively disinfected pupae (Figure 4A; GLM: LR χ2 = 31.32, df = 1, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: By preventing the pathogen from completing its lifecycle, destructive disinfection stops intra-colony disease transmission.
claims.source: We therefore concluded that by preventing the pathogen from completing its lifecycle destructive disinfection stops intra-colony disease transmission (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing no transmission from disinfected pupae.

claims.claim: Ants do not only avoid, groom and isolate pathogens but can detect and eliminate infections developing inside the bodies of their nestmates, even before they have shown external disease symptoms.
claims.source: These findings show that ants do not only avoid, groom and isolate pathogens (Cremer et al., 2007; Cremer et al., 2017) but can detect and eliminate infections developing inside the bodies of their nestmates, even before they have shown external disease symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings presented in the study.

claims.claim: The use of ant poison as an internal disinfectant within the body of others during destructive disinfection is a novel finding.
claims.source: Whilst the role of ant poison as a topical disinfectant by ants and other animals (i.e. 'anting' behaviour in birds) is well characterised (Clayton et al., 2010; Verderane et al., 2007; Tragust, 2016), its use as an internal disinfectant within the body of others during destructive disinfection is a novel and a rare example of the kill-component of social immunity (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim contrasts the novel findings with established knowledge from citations.

claims.claim: Eliminating infected kin to protect the rest of the group has been observed in termites and honeybees as well.
claims.source: Eliminating infected kin to protect the rest of the group, observed in termites and honeybees as well (Rothenbuhler, 1964; Chouvenc and Su, 2012; Spivak and Gilliam, 1998), requires an unconditional level of altruism that is expected to be absent or at least rare in other forms of sociality (e.g. aggregations, non-superorganismal family groups and communal breeders [Cremer et al., 2017]), but has parallels to the immune system of the metazoan body (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in other social insects.

claims.claim: Both the immune system and social immunity have first lines of defences that reduce the risk of infection.
claims.source: Both the immune system and social immunity have first lines of defences that reduce the risk of infection: pathogens that enter the body are met with mechanical and chemical defences, such as ciliated cells in the lung that move pathogens trapped in mucus out of the body (Cremer and Sixt, 2009), and in ants, sanitary care plays an analogous role (Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative analysis drawing on established knowledge from citations.

claims.claim: If a pathogen circumvents first defences in the body and an infection occurs, the second line of defence is often a targeted elimination of the infected cells.
claims.source: However, if a pathogen circumvents these first defences in the body and an infection occurs, the second line of defence is often a targeted elimination of the infected cells.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about immune system function.

claims.claim: Immune cells detect an infection and transport cell death-inducing and antimicrobial compounds into infected cells by creating pores in their membrane.
claims.source: This starts with immune cells detecting an infection and then transporting cell death-inducing and antimicrobial compounds into infected cells by creating pores in their membrane (Walch et al., 2014; Kägi et al., 1994; Chowdhury and Lieberman, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about immune cell function, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ants unpack infected pupae and make perforations in their cuticle, enabling them to spray poison directly into the pupae's body, displaying mechanisms analogous to immune cell elimination.
claims.source: Likewise, our experiments revealed that ants unpack infected pupae and make perforations in their cuticle, enabling the ants to spray their poison directly into the pupae's body; hence they display mechanisms analogous to immune cell elimination.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the experimental findings and knowledge of immune function.

claims.claim: The second line of defence destroys the infected cell/insect, along with the infection, to prevent transmission.
claims.source: In both cases, this second line of defence destroys the infected cell/insect, along with the infection, to prevent transmission (Shore et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement about immune and social immunity function, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The loss of both somatic cells and individual insect workers can be tolerated with negligible effects on fitness.
claims.source: Since the loss of both somatic cells and individual insect workers can be tolerated with negligible effects on fitness (Cremer and Sixt, 2009), these convergent strategies have likely evolved at both the multicellular and superorganismal levels of biological organisation, as an effective way to clear infections and avoid any further damage to the body and colony, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about fitness effects, supported by citation.

claims.claim: These convergent strategies have likely evolved at both the multicellular and superorganismal levels of biological organisation as an effective way to clear infections.

results.result: Ants detect infected pupae during the pathogen's non-contagious incubation period using chemical 'sickness cues'. Unpacking behavior occurs 2-10 days after pathogen exposure in a dose-dependent manner, with 85% of unpacked pupae harboring lethal infections while only 25% of non-unpacked pupae were infected.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 provide strong experimental evidence with appropriate statistical tests (Cox proportional hazards regression, GLM) showing dose-dependent unpacking behavior and high infection rates in unpacked pupae. The timing data (C36, C41) and CFU measurements (C37) confirm detection occurs during the non-contagious incubation period. Chemical detection is supported by pentane washing experiments (C4, C46-C48).

results.result: Destructive disinfection consists of three behavioral components: unpacking pupae from cocoons, biting to perforate cuticles, and poison spraying. After unpacking, ants increase poison spraying 15-fold and double grooming duration compared to sanitary care, resulting in pupal death and heavily damaged corpses coated in poison.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 provide quantitative behavioral data with appropriate statistical tests (GLMM, LMER) showing significant increases in all three behaviors. The multicomponent nature is well-documented through behavioral observations and measurements (C45). The data clearly distinguish destructive disinfection from sanitary care.

results.result: Infected pupae exhibit distinct chemical profiles characterized by increased abundances of specific cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs). Eight out of 24 CHCs showed higher relative abundances on unpacked pupae, with four CHCs specifically elevated compared to both control and cocooned pupae. These chemical differences are of pupal origin, not fungal-derived.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 are supported by rigorous GC-MS chemical analysis with appropriate statistical tests (perMANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis). The pentane washing experiment (C46) provides functional evidence that CHCs are necessary for detection. The comparative analysis of fungal and pupal profiles (C50-C52) convincingly demonstrates pupal origin of the chemical signals.

results.result: Injection of β-1,3-glucans (fungal immune elicitor) induces immune gene expression and increases abundance of two CHCs (Tritriacontadiene and Tritriacontene) that are also elevated on Metarhizium-infected pupae. This links chemical profile changes to host immune responses rather than direct fungal products.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 provide experimental evidence with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U, LMER) showing immune gene upregulation and CHC changes following β-glucan injection. The overlap between β-glucan-induced and infection-induced CHC changes (C61) supports the mechanistic link. However, only 2 of 4 key CHCs were replicated, suggesting partial rather than complete mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Destructive disinfection prevents pathogen replication through synergistic interaction of three components: unpacking, biting, and poison application. The behavior reduced sporulation by 65% after 1 day and 95% after 5 days. All three components are necessary and must be performed in sequence, with poison being the active antimicrobial agent that requires cocoon removal and cuticle perforation to reach internal infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 are supported by well-designed in vitro experiments with full factorial design and appropriate statistics (GLM with interaction terms). The time-dependent (C63-C64) and group-size effects (C66) are consistent with poison being the limiting factor (C71-C72). The experimental design properly isolates each component's contribution.

results.result: Destructive disinfection prevents intra-colony disease transmission by stopping the pathogen lifecycle. Sporulating pupae caused lethal infections in 42% of exposed ants, while destructively disinfected pupae caused no disease transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 provide direct experimental evidence with appropriate statistical tests (GLM) showing complete prevention of disease transmission from disinfected pupae. The experimental design properly tests the colony-level impact by exposing ants to treated versus untreated infected pupae.

results.result: Destructive disinfection in ant colonies operates analogously to cellular immune responses in multicellular organisms. Both systems detect infections early and eliminate infected units (cells or individuals) through targeted delivery of antimicrobial compounds via membrane/cuticle perforation, representing convergent evolution at different levels of biological organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 draw analogies between ant social immunity and cellular immunity based on mechanistic similarities (detection, perforation, antimicrobial delivery). While the parallels are conceptually interesting and supported by citations, the claim of convergent evolution (C86) is speculative. The analogy is logical but lacks direct evolutionary evidence or phylogenetic analysis to demonstrate independent evolution of similar mechanisms.

results.result: The chemical cues used for infection detection are distinct from corpse removal signals, consist of low-volatility long-chain CHCs requiring close contact, and may represent evolutionarily conserved 'sickness cues' in Hymenopteran social insects. Two of the four key CHCs are also elevated in infected honeybees, suggesting conservation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by citations and chemical data showing distinctness from corpse signals. The low-volatility properties (C91) are supported by chemical analysis and citations. However, claims of evolutionary conservation (C94-C95) are speculative, based on limited cross-species comparison (only honeybees cited in C93). The functional interpretation (C92, C96-C97) is logical but lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: The high effectiveness of destructive disinfection (95% prevention of transmission) explains why generalist fungal pathogens like Metarhizium do not cause colony-wide epidemics in ants despite being common in field populations. This selective pressure may have driven evolution of host manipulation in specialist ant-pathogenic fungi.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is directly supported by experimental data. However, claims C99-C103 are speculative inferences about field epidemiology and evolutionary dynamics. While the logic is sound and supported by citations, there is no direct field data demonstrating that destructive disinfection prevents epidemics in natural populations, nor phylogenetic evidence for the proposed evolutionary scenario with specialist fungi.

results.result: Destructive disinfection behavior is observed in multiple Lasius populations and species, including an unrelated L. neglectus supercolony from Jena and the non-supercolonial species L. niger, suggesting it may be a common behavior in the genus Lasius.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C129-C130 provide observational data from additional populations and species showing similar destructive disinfection behavior. The data show high rates of destructive disinfection in pathogen-exposed pupae (>60% in Jena, 95% in L. niger) and no unpacking of controls. This supports generalizability within Lasius, though the broader claim about other ant genera (C105) remains speculative.

results.result: Destructive disinfection likely evolved in ants because their sedentary, territorial lifestyle and midden waste management create persistent disease transmission risks. This contrasts with honeybees (random corpse disposal during flight) and termites (cannibalism with gut neutralization), representing convergent solutions to the shared selective pressure of eliminating infected individuals early.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 about ant ecology are well-supported by citations. The comparative analysis with honeybees (C111) and termites (C112-C113) is supported by citations. However, the evolutionary inference (C106, C114) is speculative, lacking direct evidence that midden risks drove evolution of destructive disinfection. The comparative framework is logical but the specific evolutionary claims are not directly tested.

results.result: Social animals face elevated disease risks due to frequent interactions, leading to evolution of disease detection and avoidance behaviors. In closely related groups, selection may favor both detection by healthy individuals and advertisement of disease status by sick individuals when this benefits kin.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C17 are theoretical predictions from evolutionary immunology and disease ecology, well-supported by multiple citations to established literature. These provide the conceptual framework for the study but are not novel findings. They represent accepted theory rather than new empirical results.

results.result: Social insect colonies are superorganisms with irreversible reproductive division of labor, where natural selection acts at the colony level. They have evolved social immunity including sanitary care, characterized by a care-kill dichotomy, though the kill-component and responses to established infections remain poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are established knowledge about social insect biology and social immunity, well-supported by citations. Claim C27 identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study. These claims provide essential background context but are not novel findings from this work.

results.result: The study system consists of the invasive ant Lasius neglectus and the generalist fungal pathogen Metarhizium brunneum. Metarhizium penetrates host cuticle within 24-48 hours, undergoes a 1-2 day non-infectious incubation period, then sporulates 1-3 days after host death, releasing millions of infectious spores. The experimental exposure procedure delivered ~1800 spores per pupa, with ~95 reaching the pupa inside the cocoon.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33, C119-C128 describe the study system and methods. The pathogen biology (C31-C33) is established knowledge supported by citations. The study organism characteristics (C119-C120) are supported by citations. The exposure methodology (C126) is supported by experimental measurements. These are methodological details rather than novel findings.
